A tram is a passenger vehicle that runs on metal rails (tracks) laid directly into a city street, powered by electricity. Think of it as a cross between a bus and a train — it carries people from stop to stop through a city, but it moves along a fixed track rather than steering freely like a bus.

A tram is a long, boxy vehicle, somewhat like a bus in shape, but it sits on metal wheels that grip steel rails set into the road. Most trams have large windows, sliding doors on the sides, and rows of seats inside. They can be a single car or several cars joined together (like a short train). Above the tram, you will often see a thin metal arm reaching up to touch an overhead electric wire — this is how the tram draws its power.

A tram is electrically powered. The overhead wires (called the catenary or overhead line) carry electricity. The tram's arm — called a pantograph or trolley pole — stays in constant contact with this wire while the tram moves, drawing power continuously, the same way a phone charges from a cable. Because of this, a tram cannot steer around the wire; it must follow its fixed route.

The rails are embedded flush into the road surface, so they do not rise above the ground. Cars, cyclists, and pedestrians cross over these rails all the time — trams share the street with everyone else.
What it does and where you find it

A tram is a form of public transport in cities and towns. It travels along a fixed, numbered route, stopping at designated points called tram stops to let passengers board and alight (get on and get off). You pay a fare to ride it, just as you would on a bus. Trams run frequently — often every few minutes — and are designed to move large numbers of people efficiently through busy urban areas.

You are most likely to see trams in European cities (Amsterdam, Lisbon, Zürich, Vienna, Melbourne in Australia), where many cities kept their tram networks running for over a century. Some cities removed their trams in the mid-20th century and later brought them back in modernised form.
How a tram is different from similar vehicles

Understanding what a tram is not makes its identity much clearer:

Tram vs. Train
A train runs on its own dedicated tracks, completely separated from road traffic — through countryside, tunnels, or on elevated structures. A tram runs on the street itself, among cars and pedestrians. Trains travel faster and cover greater distances; trams are slower and move through the heart of a city.

Tram vs. Bus
A bus has rubber tyres and can steer anywhere on the road. A tram has metal wheels and can only follow its fixed rails — it cannot turn or deviate. A bus can be rerouted if a road is blocked; a tram cannot. On the other hand, trams are smoother, quieter, and can carry far more passengers per vehicle than a bus.

Tram vs. Metro / Subway / Underground
A metro runs underground (or on elevated tracks) in a completely separate system from street traffic. It has its own tunnels and platforms. A tram runs at ground level, in the open, on the same street as everyone else. This means a tram can be slowed down by traffic jams, red lights, or pedestrians — a metro is not affected by any of that.

Tram vs. Light Rail
"Light rail" is a modern term that is very closely related to trams. Light rail vehicles often look identical to trams. The difference is mostly operational: light rail systems sometimes run on their own dedicated corridor (not shared with traffic) for part of the route, which lets them go faster. In everyday language, many people use "tram" and "light rail" interchangeably, and the line between them is blurry.

The word "tram" is the standard term in British English and is used widely across Europe, Australia, and much of the world.

In the United States, the same vehicle is usually called a streetcar or trolley (or "trolley car"). So if an American says "trolley," they almost certainly mean what a British person would call a "tram."

1. Aerial tram (also called a cable car or gondola)
In some places — especially in the United States — "tram" also refers to an enclosed cabin that is suspended from a thick overhead cable and travels between two fixed points, often up the side of a mountain or across a gorge. The cabin hangs in the air and is pulled along the cable by a motor. You may hear "aerial tram," "tramway," or simply "tram" for this. Famous examples include mountain resort trams and urban aerial tramways like the Roosevelt Island Tram in New York City.

2. Mining tram
In industrial or historical contexts, a "tram" can refer to a small, low, open wagon that runs on narrow rails inside a mine or quarry. Workers and materials are moved through underground tunnels using these wagons. This usage is older and you are less likely to encounter it in everyday conversation, but it appears in historical texts and mining literature.
Quick mental image to lock it in

Picture a city street. Embedded in the road are two shining metal rails running from one end of the street to the other. Along those rails glides a long, sleek, electrically-powered vehicle — something like a bus, but heavier, smoother, and quieter. It stops at marked spots on the pavement, its doors open, people step on and off, and it hums away along its fixed path. That vehicle is a tram.
Related words you will likely encounter

• Tramway — the entire system of tracks and routes that trams use; also the organization that runs them
  • Tram stop — a designated place where trams stop to pick up passengers (like a bus stop, but for trams)
  • Tram line — a specific route that a tram follows (e.g., "Take tram line 4 to the city centre")
  • Tramcar — another word for a single tram vehicle (more formal/old-fashioned)
  • Streetcar / Trolley — the American English equivalents of "tram"
  • Catenary — the overhead electric wire that powers the tram
